en.summary: This chapter defines war as a matter of national survival and human life. It argues that decisions should be founded on five factors—Way, Heaven, Earth, commander, and law—and then compared by seven calculations. Comparison is not a static score but a means to find usable advantages and to form plans that seize initiative. Deception and measures of perception serve information and cognition, yet everything returns to prewar calculation: the more complete the conditions, preparations, and judgments, the more foreseeable the outcome.
en.seoTitle: Laying Plans: Five Factors and Seven Calculations
en.seoDescription: War is a state's gravest matter; assess five factors and seven calculations. Thorough prewar calculation makes victory more predictable.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: Warfare is the great affair of state, the matter of life and death, the road to survival or ruin; it must not be neglected. Therefore it is to be examined by five factors and compared by seven calculations to determine the facts: first, the Way; second, Heaven; third, Earth; fourth, the commander; fifth, method and discipline.

By the Way I mean the people being in harmony with their ruler, willing to live and die with him and unafraid of danger. By Heaven I mean yin and yang, cold and heat, and the timing of the seasons. By Earth I mean distances and terrain—high and low, near and far, dangerous and safe, wide and narrow, and grounds of life and death. By the commander I mean wisdom, trustworthiness, benevolence, courage, and strictness. By method and discipline I mean organization, the chain of command, and the control of expenditure. Every commander has heard of these five things; the one who understands them will win, and the one who does not will not. Therefore compare them by seven calculations to learn the truth: Which sovereign has the Way? Which commander is capable? Which side has Heaven and Earth in its favor? Which side enforces laws and orders? Which has stronger forces? Which has better-trained troops? Which has clearer rewards and punishments? By these I know who will win and who will lose.

If a commander listens to my plan and employs it, retain him; if he does not listen to my plan and will surely fail in employing it, dismiss him. Calculate the advantages and secure his adherence; then create strategic momentum to support operations beyond the immediate theater. Momentum is shaping power in response to advantage. Warfare is the way of deception. Therefore, when able, appear unable; when employing forces, appear not to; when near, appear far; when far, appear near. Offer bait in the form of gain; exploit disorder; attack where the enemy is unprepared; prepare against an enemy whose forces are sound; avoid one who is strong. Anger them and throw them into confusion; humble yourself to make them arrogant; give them no rest when they are at ease; divide those who are united. Attack where they are unprepared; appear where you are not expected. This is the victory of the military strategist, and it must not be disclosed beforehand.

Those who are victorious before battle have made many calculations; those not victorious have made few. Many calculations bring victory; few calculations do not bring victory—how much less for those who make none? From this observation I can see who will win.

points.title: Warfare is a state's great affair
points.body: War must not be treated as a commander's personal gamble. It involves public resources, life and death, and the survival of the state, so it requires careful assessment above all.

points.title: Five factors and seven calculations
points.body: The five factors provide observational dimensions and the seven calculations require step-by-step comparison of enemy and self. Together they form the basic framework for prewar judgment.

points.title: Create momentum by exploiting advantage
points.body: Plans must be adjusted to present opportunities and constraints; 'momentum' is not arbitrary change but shaping the situation by leveraging concrete advantages.

points.title: Deception and shaping perceptions
points.body: Presenting ability as inability, use as disuse, nearness as distance and vice versa serves to mislead the opponent and expose exploitable openings.

points.title: Prewar calculation creates victory
points.body: True advantage is formed before combat. The difference between many calculations and few lies in whether conditions have been fully inventoried and compared.

en.summary: This chapter focuses on the timing and costs of war. Once an army is mobilized, transport, equipment, levies and rising prices steadily drain national resources; even a well-devised tactical plan can be nullified by delay. Therefore the use of arms prizes swift achievement of objectives and the shortening of supply lines. The capture of enemy resources and personnel should be treated not only as plunder but as rewards, reorganization, and conversion so that defeating the enemy also strengthens your own forces.
en.seoTitle: Waging War — Cost, Speed and Logistics (Sun Tzu, Ch.2)
en.seoDescription: Explains why swift victories and using enemy supplies preserve the state; prolonged campaigns drain wealth and blunt forces.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In matters of warfare, when chariots are driven by thousands, wagons numbered by the hundreds, armored men amounting to a hundred thousand, and provisions must be supplied for a thousand li, then internal and external expenses, the costs for guests, materials like glue and lacquer, and the provision and maintenance of chariots and armor will come to a daily cost of a thousand pieces of gold; only then can an army of one hundred thousand be raised. In the employment of arms, what matters most is victory; if the campaign is prolonged, weapons grow blunt and edge is lost, assaults on cities sap strength, and long exposure of troops exhausts the state's resources. When weapons are dulled and edge lost, when strength is bent and treasure spent, feudal lords seize the opportunity to rise; even the wise cannot remedy what follows. Hence among soldiers one hears praise of clumsy speed but not of skilful delay. There has never been a case where protracted warfare benefited the state. Therefore one who does not fully understand the harms of using arms cannot fully understand their benefits.

A competent commander does not levy the same men twice nor requisition grain for three successive years; he takes what is needed from his own state only as necessary and lives off the enemy's supplies, and so the army's rations will suffice.

When a state's army is provisioned from afar, long transport impoverishes the people; when the army is close, prices rise and people are forced to sell at high cost, exhausting their wealth and driving them into corvée. Strength is strained and the treasury exhausted; the heartland and households lie empty. Of the people's resources, seven tenths are consumed; of the public's resources—broken carts and idle horses, armor, arrows and crossbows, halberds, shields, siege engines, draft oxen and large wagons—six tenths are consumed.
Therefore a wise general strives to feed his troops from the enemy: one measure taken from the enemy may be worth twenty of ours; one bundle of their straw may be worth twenty of ours.

Killing the enemy comes from anger; taking the enemy's goods is profit. Thus in chariot battles, when you capture ten or more chariots, reward those who captured them first and replace the captured banners. Mix captured chariots into your own ranks, use competent captured soldiers and feed them well—this is called defeating the enemy and increasing your strength.
Hence in war what is prized is victory, not duration. Therefore the general who understands warfare holds the people's lives in his hands and is the arbiter of the state's safety and peril.

points.title: Victory matters; not duration
points.body: This chapter does not urge recklessness. It argues that prolonged consumption dulls weapons, saps strength and treasure, and gives rivals opportunity to act.

points.title: Know the harms of warfare
points.body: Focusing only on potential gains without accounting for direct and indirect costs is insufficient for deciding to wage war. Risk awareness is prerequisite to benefit assessment.

points.title: Live off the enemy
points.body: Long-range supply burdens the populace. Shortening supply lines and using local or enemy resources reduces the total cost of war.

points.title: Defeat the enemy and grow stronger
points.body: After capturing enemy chariots, replace their insignia, integrate their vehicles and troops, and treat captured soldiers well—this converts enemy assets into your own strength.

en.summary: This chapter presents a doctrine of achieving victory while preserving the whole. The highest form of success is not triumph in open battle but first undermining the enemy's plans and alliances so they cannot resist; besieging cities is a last resort because of its cost. The chapter also treats comparisons of force, the ruler–general relationship, and the conditions for knowing victory, stressing that political leaders should not interfere with military expertise and that commanders must grasp enemy and self, size and disposition of forces, timing, and the will of the organization.
en.seoTitle: Attack by Stratagem — Sun Tzu on Complete Victory (Chapter 3)
en.seoDescription: Ranks methods of victory—undermine plans and alliances before fighting; siege is last resort. Emphasizes unity, judgment, and noninterference.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In the methods of warfare, preserving the state is supreme; destroying the state is next. Preserving the army is supreme; destroying the army is next. Preserving a division is supreme; destroying a division is next. Preserving a regiment is supreme; destroying a regiment is next. Preserving a unit is supreme; destroying a unit is next. Therefore, to win a hundred victories in a hundred engagements is not the acme of skill; to subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill.

Therefore the best strategy is to defeat the enemy's plans; next best is to disrupt their alliances; next best is to fight their armies; worst is to besiege fortified cities. Siege warfare should be undertaken only when unavoidable. To frame and fit siege-towers and battering engines, and prepare other implements, takes three months; to raise approaches and undermine the walls takes another three months. If a general cannot restrain his anger and the troops swarm like ants, killing a third of the soldiers yet failing to take the city, this is the disaster of siege warfare.

Thus the skillful commander bends the enemy's forces without fighting, captures their cities without assaulting them, ruins their state without protracted campaigns. He strives to contend for the realm with his resources intact; therefore the troops are not exhausted and the gains remain whole—this is the method of attacking by stratagem.

Hence in the conduct of war: if you are ten times as many, surround the enemy; if five times, attack; if twice, divide them; if equal, be able to fight; if fewer, be able to hold the defensive; if inferior in every way, be able to avoid them. Thus the firmness of a small force can lead to its capture by a larger one.
A commander is the state's principal support. If that support is complete, the state will be strong; if the support is flawed, the state will be weak.

Therefore there are three things by which a ruler may bring trouble upon his army: not recognizing when the army cannot advance yet ordering it to advance, and not recognizing when it cannot retreat yet ordering it to retreat—this ties the army; not understanding the matters of the three divisions yet meddling in their administration—this confuses the soldiers; not knowing the authority assigned within the three divisions yet interfering with their duties—this makes the soldiers distrustful. When the three armies are confused and distrustful, ruin for the state is near; this is called leading a disordered army to defeat.

There are five points by which victory may be known: knowing whether you can fight or cannot fight; mastering the use of many or few forces; having unity of purpose between high and low; preparing for the expected and awaiting the unexpected; and having a capable commander whom the ruler does not hamper. These five constitute the way to know victory.

Hence it is said: Know the enemy and know yourself, and you will not be imperiled in a hundred engagements. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat. If you know neither the enemy nor yourself, you will be defeated in every battle.

points.title: Subduing without battle
points.body: The highest excellence is not measured by the number of battlefield victories but by whether the objective is achieved with minimal destruction.

points.title: Best to attack the plan
points.body: Strategies are ranked: first disrupt the enemy's plans, then their alliances, then their armies; besieging cities is the least desirable option.

points.title: Strive to preserve the whole
points.body: Preservation is not passive avoidance; it means securing the state and forces so success does not require exhausting one's own resources.

points.title: Three causes of a ruler's trouble with the army
points.body: Direct interference born of ignorance about when to advance or retreat, how commands and authority are organized, will produce confusion and disorder among the troops.

points.title: Know the enemy and yourself
points.body: Knowing how to judge fightability, employ forces, ensure unity of will, prepare for surprise, and allow competent command without interference is the practical formula for victory.

en.summary: This chapter examines what can be controlled and what cannot. It argues that one should first create conditions that make oneself undefeatable—this is within one's control—while whether the enemy exposes a weakness cannot be forced. The skilled combatant does not seek glory through risky feats but chooses engagements where victory is already likely. The sequence degree → measure → calculation → comparison → victory shows how advantage arises from successive assessments of terrain, capacity, numbers, and force balance.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — Military Disposition (Chapter 4): Securing Victory
en.seoDescription: Explains making oneself undefeatable, waiting for enemy weakness, and how measurement and calculation turn terrain and forces into victory.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In former times those skilled in war first made themselves invincible, and then waited for the enemy to be vulnerable. "Invincible" depends on oneself; "vulnerable" depends on the enemy. Therefore the skillful warrior can make himself invincible but cannot make the enemy necessarily vulnerable. Thus: victory can be recognized, but it cannot be forced.

Being invincible is a matter of defense; vulnerability to defeat invites attack. To defend is to appear lacking; to attack is to possess surplus. The good defender conceals himself beneath the ninefold earth; the good attacker moves above the nine heavens—thus they can preserve themselves and secure complete victory.

To win in ways that everyone can see is not the highest skill; to win in battle and have the world call it skill is not the highest excellence. Lifting a single autumn hair is not proof of great strength; seeing the sun and moon is not proof of superior sight; hearing thunder is not proof of keen hearing.

What ancient writers called being skilled at war was winning where victory was easy. Therefore the victories of the skilled carry no name for cleverness and no claim of heroic deed. Their victories do not go wrong. "Not going wrong" means that where they place themselves they will certainly win; they win over foes already doomed. Thus the skilled commander stands on ground where he cannot be defeated and does not miss the enemy's collapse. Therefore a victorious army first secures victory and then seeks battle; a defeated army first engages in battle and then seeks victory. The effective commander cultivates the Way and preserves the laws, and so can direct matters of victory and defeat.

On military method: first measurement, second estimation, third calculation, fourth comparison, fifth victory. Terrain gives rise to measurement; measurement gives rise to estimation; estimation gives rise to calculation; calculation gives rise to comparison; comparison gives rise to victory. Thus a victorious army weighs ounces by the pound, while a defeated army weighs the pound by the ounce. The fighting of the victorious is like releasing accumulated water down a thousand-foot gorge—that is its form.

points.title: Make yourself invincible first
points.body: Secure your defenses, systems, and preparations first; then wait for external opportunities. This is risk control before pursuing returns.

points.title: Invincibility is within; vulnerability is in the enemy
points.body: Avoiding defeat is mainly under your control; defeating the opponent depends on whether they expose opportunities.

points.title: Win where victory is easy
points.body: True skill lies in choosing engagements with an existing advantage, not in courting danger to gain fame.

points.title: Victors secure advantage before fighting
points.body: Action is the culmination of an already established advantage, not the means to gamble on creating one.

points.title: Measure, estimate, calculate, compare, win
points.body: From terrain scale to capacity, troop numbers, and force comparison—victory follows layered, quantitative assessment.

en.summary: This chapter moves from organization and command to how momentum is formed. Governing a crowd as if it were a few depends on structure and signals; fighting many as if fighting few depends on formation and designation. Though combat shows endless variation, its basic elements are the recurring alternation of orthodox and unorthodox. Momentum is not an abstract spirit but the combination of position, speed, rhythm, and conditions into a releasable force. A brilliant leader does not only demand individual courage but designs the environment so that ordinary people, placed and timed correctly, produce a decisive collective effect.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu Chapter 5 — Military Momentum and the Use of Force
en.seoDescription: Explains how organization, orthodox and unorthodox tactics, timing and formation combine into decisive momentum in warfare.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: To govern many as if governing few — that is a matter of division and numbers. To fight many as if fighting few — that concerns form and designation. To marshal an army so that it will certainly engage the enemy without defeat — that lies in the use of orthodox and unorthodox tactics. Where force is applied, as when hurling a heavy stone at an egg, that concerns emptiness and solidity.

In all fighting, match with the orthodox and win by the unorthodox. Therefore the skillful user of surprise is inexhaustible like Heaven and Earth, unending like rivers and seas. They end only to begin again, like the sun and moon; they die and are reborn, like the four seasons. Sounds are not more than five, yet the changes of the five sounds cannot be fully heard; colors are not more than five, yet the variations of five colors cannot be fully seen; tastes are not more than five, yet the shifts of five tastes cannot be fully sampled. Battle formations are no more than orthodox and unorthodox, yet the variations of orthodox and unorthodox cannot be exhausted. Orthodox and unorthodox generate one another in a cycle without end — who can fully fathom it?

The swiftness of rushing water that can carry off a floating stone — that is momentum. The rapid strike of a bird of prey that can break and shatter — that is tempo. Therefore the skillful fighter’s momentum is steep, and his tempo is brief. Momentum is like a drawn crossbow; tempo is like the release mechanism.

Confused and clamorous, the contest appears chaotic yet cannot be thrown into disorder; blurred and indeterminate, the formation is rounded and cannot be broken. Disorder is born of order; timidity is born of courage; weakness is born of strength. Order and disorder are matters of organization and numbers; courage and timidity are matters of momentum; strength and weakness are matters of form.
Therefore the one who skillfully moves the enemy shapes a situation to which the enemy will respond; he offers and the enemy will take. Use advantage to move them, and await them with your troops.

Thus the skilled commander seeks victory in the situation, not by blaming his men; therefore he can choose people and assign them to fit the situation. To rely on momentum is to fight with men as if turning logs and stones. The nature of wood and stone: when level they rest, when tilted they move; when square they stop, when round they roll. Therefore the skillful commander’s momentum is like rolling a round stone down a thousand‑footh cliff — that is momentum.

points.title: Division and designation
points.body: Whether a large organization can be commanded depends on layered structure, units of responsibility, and consistent signaling.

points.title: Match orthodox, win by unorthodox
points.body: Orthodox and unorthodox are mutually transforming configurations; one should not treat either as a permanently fixed category.

points.title: Steep momentum, brief tempo
points.body: Power should be concentrated into a short, effective release—like a drawn crossbow and a quick trigger; prolonging the tempo dissipates advantage.

points.title: Shape and bait
points.body: Use visible form and offered advantages to steer the enemy’s choices, then meet their response with prepared reserves.

points.title: Seek victory in the situation, not in blame
points.body: Leadership is about selecting people and arranging conditions to exploit momentum, not simply blaming individuals for systemic failure.

en.summary: This chapter centers on seizing the initiative so that the enemy acts according to your design rather than forcing you to react. By offering advantage or harm, using speed, feints and concealment, you disperse enemy defenses and concentrate at the decisive point. The highest military form is formlessness, which prevents the enemy from knowing where to commit resources. The chapter closes with the metaphor of water: water avoids heights and flows downward; troops avoid the strong and strike the weak. Methods must not be fixed but must change with the enemy and the environment.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — Chapter 6: Emptiness and Fullness (Formlessness)
en.seoDescription: How to seize the initiative, disperse enemy defenses, concentrate forces at decisive points, and remain formless like water in order to adapt and win.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: Those who occupy the ground of battle before the enemy arrives are at ease; those who take the ground later and must hurry to battle are fatigued. Therefore the skillful commander causes others to come to him and does not go to others.

To make the enemy come of their own accord is to offer them profit; to prevent the enemy from coming is to harm them. Thus make the idle enemy labor, make the sated enemy hungry, make the secure enemy move. Move where they do not expect to go; strike where they do not expect to be struck.

To march a thousand li without fatigue is to move through ground unoccupied by men. To attack and be sure to capture is to strike where he does not guard; to defend and be sure to hold is to defend where he does not attack. Therefore the skillful attacker makes the enemy uncertain where to guard; the skillful defender makes the enemy uncertain where to attack. Subtle, subtle indeed — reaching formlessness; mysterious, mysterious indeed — reaching soundlessness. Thus one can determine the enemy’s fate.

Advance in a way that cannot be stopped by striking at their weak points; withdraw in a way that cannot be pursued by moving with speed beyond reach. Thus, if I desire battle, even though the enemy has high ramparts and deep ditches, I can force him to fight by attacking what he must relieve. If I desire not to fight, even if I merely mark out ground and hold it, I can prevent the enemy from engaging by diverting his intentions.

Therefore give the enemy a visible form while I remain formless; then I concentrate while the enemy disperses. I concentrate as one, the enemy divides into ten; when ten attack one, I am many and the enemy few. He who can use many against few makes his engagements sure. If the place where I will fight cannot be known, then the enemy must prepare in many places; with many places to prepare, the place I fight will be thinly guarded. Prepare the front and the rear will be weak; prepare the rear and the front will be weak; prepare the left and the right will be weak; prepare the right and the left will be weak. If you prepare everywhere, then nothing is weak. 'Weak' means being the one forced to guard; 'many' means making others guard against you.

Therefore, knowing where to fight and when to fight allows you to gather forces over a thousand li for battle; not knowing where or when means the left cannot help the right, the right cannot help the left, the front cannot help the rear, and the rear cannot help the front — and that is with distances of only a few li, much less dozens. In my judgment, though the Yue may have many soldiers, how much does that avail in victory or defeat? Hence it is said: victory can be seized. Even if the enemy is numerous, he can be rendered unable to fight.

Thus by calculation you know the measures of gain and loss; by disposition you know the principles of movement and stillness; by forming shape you know the ground of life and death; by probing you discover surplus and deficiency. Therefore the extreme in shaping an army is to be formless. Formless, the deepest spy cannot see it, the wisest cannot plan against it. By adapting form to secure victory, the many cannot know. All may know the apparent forms by which I win, but none know the underlying forms by which I control victory. Therefore my triumphs cannot be repeated in the same way; I shape myself endlessly to circumstances.

The shape of an army is like water. The way water moves is to avoid heights and flow downward; the army that wins avoids the strong and strikes the weak. Water shapes its course to the ground; army shapes victory to the enemy. Hence an army has no constant form, no fixed shape; one who can change with the enemy to secure victory is called divine. Likewise the five elements have no permanent victor, the four seasons have no fixed place: days are short or long, the moon wanes and waxes.

points.title: Make others come; do not go to others
points.body: Initiative is not merely acting first but forcing the enemy to respond to your timing, position and resource allocation.

points.title: Attack what they must relieve
points.body: You need not assault an opponent’s chosen strongpoint directly; change the stakes so they abandon their advantageous positions.

points.title: I concentrate while the enemy divides
points.body: Hide the main direction of your advance to force the enemy to guard many places, then concentrate locally to achieve numerical superiority at the decisive point.

points.title: The ultimate formation is formlessness
points.body: Avoid fixed, readable deployment patterns so that your informational advantage cannot be interpreted and used against you.

points.title: The army’s form is like water
points.body: Tactics must adapt to terrain and to the enemy; repeating previously successful shapes without regard to changing conditions risks failure.

en.summary: This chapter examines the difficulty of moving an army from assembly to the capture of advantageous positions. Turning a circuitous route into a direct advantage requires inducement, route planning, speed, and logistics; pursuing speed alone may cost the baggage train and divide the forces. The text presents the wind, forest, fire, and mountain modes of action, emphasizes unified signals through drums and banners, discusses morale and physical strength, and counsels restraint when facing feigned retreats, decoy forces, returning armies, and desperate foes.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — Chapter 7: Contesting Positions and Maneuver
en.seoDescription: On contesting advantageous positions through indirect routes, the wind, forest, fire, and mountain modes of action, unified signals, morale, and logistics.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In all the methods of employing troops, the general receives orders from the sovereign, combines forces and marshals the people, makes alliances and establishes camps; nothing is more difficult than contesting positions. The difficulty in contesting positions lies in making the roundabout seem direct and turning danger into advantage. Therefore take a circuitous route and lure them with profit; when those behind set out, the first arrivals will already be there—this is the strategy of indirect and direct movement.

Therefore contesting for advantage brings both profit and danger. If the whole army marches to seize an advantage, it will not arrive in time; if part of the army is sent to seize it, the baggage will be lost. Therefore roll up the armor, hurry, and do not rest by day or night; travel at double speed and march without stopping. If you contest an advantage a hundred li away, the three army commanders may be captured; the vigorous will go first and the exhausted will lag behind, so only one in ten will arrive. If you contest an advantage fifty li away, the commander of the vanguard may be lost, and only half will arrive. If you contest an advantage thirty li away, two-thirds will arrive. Therefore an army without baggage perishes; without provisions it perishes; without accumulated stores it perishes. Whoever does not know the designs of neighboring lords cannot make alliances in advance; whoever does not know the terrain of mountains, forests, obstacles, and marshes cannot march; whoever does not employ local guides cannot gain the advantage of the ground.

Thus an army is established through deception, moved by advantage, and changed by dividing and uniting. Therefore be swift as the wind, quiet as a forest, fierce as fire, immovable as a mountain, inscrutable as darkness, and sudden in action as thunder. Plunder the countryside and divide your forces; extend your territory and distribute the gains; weigh the situation and then act. Whoever is first to understand the strategy of the indirect and direct approaches will prevail—this is the method of contesting positions.

The Military Regulations say: 'When voices cannot be heard, use gongs and drums; when people cannot see one another, use standards and banners.' Gongs, drums, standards, and banners serve as the people's common ears and eyes. Once the people are unified by them, the brave cannot advance alone and the timid cannot retreat alone—this is the method of employing a multitude. Therefore night fighting uses many gongs and drums, while day fighting uses many standards and banners; this is how one alters the way people hear and see.

An army's morale can be seized, and a general's mind can be shaken. Therefore morning morale is keen, at midday it flags, and in the evening it turns homeward. The skilled commander avoids keen morale and strikes when it flags or turns homeward—this is managing morale; he uses order to await disorder and calm to await clamor—this is governing the mind; he uses proximity to await distance, ease to await toil, and fullness to await hunger—this is managing strength; he does not challenge an enemy whose standards are in perfect order or attack a formation drawn up in imposing array—this is managing change.

Therefore, in employing troops: do not advance against a high ridge; do not go against an enemy who has a hill at his back; do not pursue a feigned retreat; do not attack fresh, vigorous troops; do not swallow the bait of a decoy force; do not block an army returning home; when you surround an army, leave it an outlet; do not press a desperate enemy. These are the principles of employing troops.

points.title: Turn indirect into direct; turn danger into advantage
points.body: An indirect route that changes the enemy’s judgment and gains time can become the direct way to arrive first.

points.title: Contesting advantage brings both gain and risk
points.body: Pursuing opportunity creates speed but stretches formations and endangers supplies; advantage and risk coexist.

points.title: Wind — Forest — Fire — Mountain
points.body: Swift, still, aggressive and immobile correspond to different tempos; the point is to switch according to purpose, not to seek speed alone.

points.title: The people's common ears and eyes
points.body: Shared signals prevent the brave from advancing alone and the timid from retreating alone, turning individual reactions into organized action.

points.title: Managing morale, mind, strength and change
points.body: Waiting for the enemy’s sharpness to wane, their order to falter, and their strength to be spent before engaging is control of tempo.

en.summary: This chapter emphasizes that principles must not be detached from circumstances. Avoiding certain roads, not attacking some forces, not contesting particular cities or lands, and even refusing some sovereign commands may all be necessary to prevent mechanically applying general rules. Mature judgment sees hidden risks in apparent benefits and looks for remedies within dangers. The chapter closes by listing five dangerous character traits in commanders, showing how courage, clinging to life, impatience, excessive scrupulousness, and misplaced affection for the people can all be exploited by an opponent.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu: Nine Changes (Ch. 8) — Adaptation & Five Dangers
en.seoDescription: Chapter 8 stresses adapting rules to circumstances, weighing benefits and harms, and five character-based risks leaders must guard against.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In the methods of warfare, a commander takes orders from the sovereign, unites the forces and gathers the troops. On broken ground do not linger; at crossroads join with allies; on cut-off ground do not remain; when surrounded, devise plans; on fatal ground, fight. There are roads one must not take, armies one must not attack, cities one must not besiege, terrain one must not contest, and sovereign commands one must not accept. Therefore a general who understands how to exploit the advantages of the Nine Changes knows how to employ troops; a general who does not understand the advantages of the Nine Changes, though he knows the lay of the land, cannot gain its benefits; one who organizes troops without knowledge of the Nine Changes, though he knows the terrain's advantages, cannot make effective use of his men.

Therefore the wise man's deliberations always mix considerations of benefit and harm: mixed with benefit he attends to what is attainable; mixed with harm he seeks dangers that can be resolved. Thus one bends the feudal lords by pointing to harms, conscripts them by appealing to obligations, and draws them forward by offering benefits.

Hence in the art of war do not rely on the enemy not coming; rely on being prepared to meet him. Do not rely on him not attacking; rely on possessing positions or conditions that cannot be successfully attacked.

Therefore a general has five dangers: one who resigns himself to death can be slain; one who clings to life can be captured; one quick to anger can be despised; one overly punctilious in integrity can be humiliated; one too fond of his people can become burdened. These five are a commander's faults and the disasters of employing troops. When an army is overturned and a general killed, it is always because of one of these five dangers; they must not be neglected.

points.title: Restraint in Action
points.body: Roads, enemy forces, cities, terrain, and orders should not be acted on merely because they exist; action must serve the overall objective.

points.title: Mastery of the Nine Changes
points.body: Knowing terrain is not the same as leveraging it; one must also know when to alter normal practice.

points.title: Weighing Benefits and Harms
points.body: In considering advantages, include potential harms; in assessing risks, look for solvable aspects—avoid one-sided judgment.

points.title: Do Not Rely on Enemy Inaction
points.body: Security must not be built on expecting the opponent to do nothing; it must be built on readiness to meet action.

points.title: The General's Five Dangers
points.body: Virtues taken to extremes become predictable weaknesses. Self-awareness is an element of strategic risk management.

en.summary: This chapter begins with how an army should occupy mountain, water, marsh and plain positions, then explains how to judge situations from subtle signs. Movements of trees, rising birds, dust, words, rewards and punishments, and soldiers’ postures must be read together. The chapter closes by linking organizational discipline with loyalty: punish men before they are attached and they will not accept it; if men are attached but punishment is not enforced, they are unusable. Orders must be consistent to build trust.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — Marching: Terrain, Signs, Discipline
en.seoDescription: Guidance on choosing terrain, reading battlefield signs, and balancing discipline with trust in Sun Tzu's 'Marching'.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In placing an army opposite the enemy, if mountains cut you off and you rely on valleys, occupy the high ground with observation; fight from a raised position without having to climb—this is the mountain army. If water cuts you off, keep well away from it; if the enemy is cut off by water and comes, do not meet him in the water—let him be half across and strike him; this is advantageous. If you seek battle, do not attach yourself to the water to meet the enemy; take high ground with observation and do not face the current—this is the army on the water. If marshes cut you off, depart quickly and do not linger; when armies meet amid marsh they must rely on water grasses and have their backs to dense trees—this is the marsh army. On flat ground it is easy; the right is backed and high, the front is death and the rear life—this is the plain army. The advantages of these four dispositions are how the Yellow Emperor overcame the four rulers.

Armies prefer heights and avoid low ground; they prize the sunny side and disdain the shady; they preserve life and occupy solid ground. An army without many ailments is said to be certain to win. On hills and embankments, take the sunny side and have your right flank supported—this is the advantage troops gain from the ground. After heavy rain, when the water is turbid, those who wish to ford should wait until it clears.

Where there are sheer ravines or features called sky-wells, sky-traps, sky-nets, sky-sinks and sky-gaps, withdraw at once and do not approach. If we keep away, the enemy approaches; if we approach, the enemy falls back. Where the army is bordered by obstacles, ponds, reeds, woods or thorny thickets, be careful when covering and securing lines—these are the places ambushers inhabit.

If the enemy is near and silent, he relies on his position; if he is distant and challenges, he wants you to advance. If his place of station is easy to occupy, it is advantageous. Many trees moving mean they are coming; much grass blocking the way means doubt; birds rising mean an ambush; startled beasts mean a hidden force. Dust that rises high and sharp indicates chariots; dust low and wide indicates infantry. Scattered, spreading dust denotes woodcutters or foragers; a few going back and forth denotes a camp detail. Humble words combined with increased preparations mean advance; bold words with pressing forward mean retreat. Light chariots going out first and remaining to the side mark a formation. Those who ask for peace without agreement are plotting. Running about and deploying troops indicate a set plan for engagement. Half advance and half retreat is a lure. One who stands with a staff is hungry; one who draws water and drinks first is thirsty. Those who see gain but do not advance are weary. Birds gathering indicate emptiness; cries at night indicate fear. An army in disorder shows the commander is not respected; moving banners show confusion; angry officers show fatigue. When there is grain, horses and meat, no supply rope hung, and the troops do not return to their quarters, these are desperate enemy bands. Long-winded, whispering, and speaking slowly to people indicate loss of the troops. Frequent rewards show constraint; frequent punishments show distress. To be violent first and then fear one’s own men is lack of thoroughness. Those who come to surrender and thank you seek rest. If soldiers angrily go out to meet each other and, after long time, neither join nor part, you must examine the situation carefully.

Therefore troops are not valuable merely for their numbers. What matters is avoiding reckless advance, and being able to combine forces, judge the enemy, and take prisoners. Those who are careless and readily engage the enemy will surely be captured.

If soldiers are not yet attached and you punish them, they will not accept it and will be hard to use. If soldiers are attached but punishments are not enforced, they cannot be used. Therefore govern them with regulations and align them with military discipline—this is what secures success. If commands are habitually practiced and used to teach the people, the people obey; if commands are habitually not practiced and used to teach the people, the people do not obey. Orders that are habitually observed are in harmony with the masses.

points.title: Positioning and observing
points.body: Marching involves both choosing secure positions and observing the enemy; terrain handling and intelligence interpretation are inseparable.

points.title: Prefer heights, avoid low ground
points.body: Choosing a camp values visibility, dryness, health and logistical support to minimize noncombat losses.

points.title: Read signs in context
points.body: Natural and human signals are ambiguous; never interpret them in isolation—cross-check distance, posture, dust and words.

points.title: Numbers alone do not win
points.body: Quantity is not the sole advantage; the ability to combine forces, evaluate the enemy and secure obedience matters more than merely adding men.

points.title: Rule with civility, align with force
points.body: Care and attachment build loyalty; discipline enforces cohesion. Both are necessary—either missing makes troops unusable.

en.summary: This chapter first categorizes six kinds of ground—accessible, entangling, intermediate, narrow, precipitous, and distant—and then enumerates six forms of defeat: flight, laxity, entrapment, collapse, disorder, and rout. The first set are external conditions; the second set mostly arise from errors in command and organization and should not be blamed on Heaven. Commanders must judge independently, based on enemy, own forces, and terrain, whether to fight, prioritizing the protection of the people and the state's interest. Loving and protecting troops must be paired with effective command; otherwise affection becomes indulgence.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — Terrain: Six Grounds and Six Defeats (Chapter 10)
en.seoDescription: Chapter 10 explains six terrain types and six commander-caused defeats; it stresses judging terrain, protecting the people, and disciplined leadership.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: Generally, ground takes six forms: accessible, entangling, intermediate, narrow, precipitous, and distant. If I can go and the enemy can come, it is called accessible. On accessible ground, take the high sunny places first and secure your supply routes; such ground favors battle. If one can go but cannot easily return, it is called entangling. On entangling ground, if the enemy is unprepared, sallying forth brings victory; if the enemy is prepared, sallying forth will not win and return is difficult—this is unfavorable. If I sally forth and suffer while the enemy also suffers from sallying, this is intermediate ground. On intermediate ground, even if the enemy has the advantage, I do not advance; instead I draw them out, force them to extend half their force, and then strike—this is advantageous. On narrow ground, if we occupy it first we must fill it and wait for the enemy; if the enemy occupies it first, then if they have filled it we must not follow, but if they have not filled it we may follow. On precipitous ground, if we occupy it first we must hold the high sunny places to await the enemy; if the enemy occupies it first, draw off and do not follow. On distant ground, when forces are even it is difficult to provoke battle; fighting there is disadvantageous. These six are the ways of terrain; they are the supreme responsibilities of a general and must not be overlooked.

Therefore there are troops that flee, troops that slacken, troops that are trapped, troops that collapse, troops that fall into disorder, and troops that are put to flight. These six failures are not calamities sent by Heaven but faults of the general. When forces are evenly matched yet a detachment acts alone and causes flight, it is called flight. When the soldiers are strong but the officers weak, this is laxity. When the officers are strong but the soldiers weak, this is entrapment. When senior officers are angry and refuse orders, meeting the enemy by charging on their own and the commander cannot gauge their capacity, this is collapse. When a general is weak and not strict, when training and regulations are unclear, officers and soldiers irregular, and deployments scattered and confused, this is disorder. When a general cannot assess the enemy, joins small forces against many, sends the weak to attack the strong, and troops are sent without selecting the vanguard, this results in rout. These six are the paths to defeat; they are the supreme duties of a general and must be carefully examined.

Terrain is the army’s aid. Estimating the enemy and securing victory, calculating difficulties, perils, and distances—this is the master’s way of command. One who knows this and fights will certainly win; one who does not know this and fights will certainly be defeated. Therefore, if the way of battle promises victory, then even if the ruler says 'do not fight' one can fight; if the way of battle does not promise victory, then even if the ruler orders 'fight' one should not. Thus advance without seeking fame and retreat without avoiding blame; care only to protect the people and ensure gains align with the sovereign—this is the nation's treasure.

Treat your soldiers like newborn infants, and you can have them cross deep streams with you; treat them like cherished sons, and you can die with them. To be lavish in care but unable to use them, to love them but be unable to command, to pamper and yet be unable to govern—this is like a spoiled child and is not fit for service.

Knowing that my troops can strike while not knowing that the enemy cannot be attacked is half a victory; knowing that the enemy can be attacked while not knowing that my troops cannot attack is half a victory; knowing both enemy and my troops can fight while not knowing that the ground is unsuited to battle is half a victory. Therefore the skilled commander moves without confusion and acts without exhaustion. Hence: know the enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will never be in peril; know the heavens and the earth, and your victory will be complete.

points.title: The six kinds of ground
points.body: The same terrain is not inherently advantageous to either side; what matters are who occupies it first, supply lines, ease of withdrawal, and whether forces are proportionate to the terrain.

points.title: Six defeats lie with the commander
points.body: Flight, laxity, entrapment, collapse, disorder, and rout mostly stem from misusing forces, imbalances of authority, and unclear orders—these are matters of management and leadership responsibility.

points.title: Advance without seeking fame, retreat without avoiding blame
points.body: Decisions must be professional and detached from personal reputation; priority is protecting the people and serving the state's interest.

points.title: Love must be paired with command
points.body: Trust and care cannot replace clear orders; indulgent affection without governance turns troops into spoiled dependents.

points.title: Know heaven and earth to complete victory
points.body: Knowing only the enemy and oneself is insufficient; incorporating terrain and timing into judgment raises the chance of total victory.

en.summary: This chapter distinguishes nine kinds of ground—scattered, light, contentious, intersecting, main-road, serious, difficult, encircled, and death—and prescribes different principles for each situation. Deep penetration into enemy territory alters soldiers’ psychology and unit cohesion; commanders must align will, secure supply, and control information. The serpent analogy shows how mutual rescue between front and rear creates systemic responsiveness. The point is not rote memorization of nine names but understanding how position, lines of retreat, resources and morale jointly change what to do.
en.seoDescription: Chapter 11 categorizes nine battlefield situations and shows how position, supply and morale dictate command and action.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In the methods of employing troops there are nine kinds of ground: scattered ground, light ground, contentious ground, intersecting ground, main-road ground, serious ground, difficult ground, encircled ground, and death ground. When a state fights within its own territory, that is scattered ground. When one enters another’s territory but not deeply, that is light ground. Ground that benefits both sides when either gains it is contentious ground. Ground that I can go to and the enemy can come to is intersecting ground. Where a state’s territory branches in three directions, and the first to arrive secures the larger number of people, that is main-road ground. When one penetrates deeply into another’s land and has many cities to his rear, that is serious ground. Mountain forests, obstacles, marshes and all difficult routes are difficult ground. Where the approach is narrow and the return route roundabout, and the enemy in smaller force can strike our larger force, that is encircled ground. Where swift battle preserves life but delay destroys it, that is death ground. Therefore on scattered ground there is no fighting; on light ground there is no lingering; on contentious ground there is no direct attack; on intersecting ground there is no severance; on main-road ground forces converge and join; on serious ground there is plundering; on difficult ground there is movement; on encircled ground there must be stratagem; on death ground there must be fighting.

The ancient masters of war could make it so that the enemy’s front and rear could not aid each other, the many and the few could not depend on each other, the high and the low could not rescue each other, the upper and lower could not gather; troops would separate and not assemble, units would combine without alignment. Move when it is to your advantage; stop when it is not. Asked: “If the enemy comes with massed, orderly forces, how should one wait?” The answer: “First seize what he loves, and he will obey.” Therefore speed is the ruling factor in warfare: take advantage of the enemy’s lack of preparedness, go by unexpected routes, and attack where he is unguarded.

The way of the invading force is that the deeper it goes the more it concentrates; the home ruler cannot withstand it. Forage in abundant countryside so the three armies have enough to eat. Tend them carefully and do not overwork them; conserve spirit and accumulate strength; employ movement and stratagem so that the enemy cannot predict. Drive them so they have nowhere to go, and they will fight to the death. If they cannot die, the soldiers will give their utmost. When troops are very pressed they are fearless; with nowhere to go they stand firm; deeply inside enemy territory they feel constrained; if there is no alternative they will fight. Thus their troops can be alert without drill, obtain without asking, attach without promise, and trust without orders. Remove omens and expel doubt; when death is the only road there is nowhere else to go. My soldiers without private property do not disdain wealth; without spare life they do not disdain longevity. On the day of departure, seated soldiers weep on their collars and those who lie down shed tears along their cheeks. Those driven with nowhere to turn display the courage of Zhu and Gui.

Therefore the skillful commander is likened to a single living organism. The comparison is to the serpent of Changshan: strike its head and the tail comes; strike its tail and the head comes; strike it in the middle and both head and tail come together. Asked: “Can troops be made to act like that serpent?” The answer: “Yes. The peoples of Wu and Yue hated each other, yet when they shared a boat in a storm they rescued one another like left and right hands.” Hence a harnessed chariot with its wheels buried is not yet reliable; common courage like one is the way of governance; both firmness and flexibility depend on terrain. The skilled commander binds hands so they act like one man when necessity demands it.

The affairs of the general require calm secrecy, correctness and order. He must dull the soldiers’ ears and eyes so they have no knowledge; change their duties and alter their plans so people cannot perceive; change their billets and lengthen their routes so they cannot calculate. When the commander departs, remove the ladder as one who climbs a height; when he leads them deep into the enemy’s country and then reveals his purpose, he burns the boats and breaks the kettles—like driving a flock of sheep. Drive them forward and drive them back so no one knows where they are bound. Gather the three armies and hurl them into danger: that is the work of the general. The transformations of the nine grounds, the gains of extension and contraction, and the principles of human feeling must all be observed.

In general, as a guest: deep implies concentration, shallow implies dispersion. When an army leaves its country and crosses a border, that is absolute ground; where roads reach in all directions, that is main-road ground; where one goes deep, that is serious ground; where one goes shallow, that is light ground; when rear is secure but front is narrow, that is encircled ground; when there is nowhere to go, that is death ground. Therefore on scattered ground I will unite their will; on light ground I will make them belonging; on contentious ground I will press from the rear; on intersecting ground I will guard carefully; on main-road ground I will secure the junctions; on serious ground I will maintain their supplies; on difficult ground I will improve the routes; on encircled ground I will block their gaps; on death ground I will show them there is no life. Thus the condition of troops: when surrounded, defend; when forced, fight; when past, pursue.

Therefore one who does not know the counsels of the princes cannot make plans for alliances in advance; one who does not know mountain forests, difficult passes and marsh forms cannot march an army; one who does not use local guides cannot gain the ground advantage. If four or five of these are lacking and one does not know even one, that is not the army of a hegemon. The hegemon’s army, when attacking a great state, prevents its forces from gathering; with威 impressed upon the enemy, their alliances cannot unite. Therefore do not contend for the world’s alliances nor cultivate sway for the world; rely on your own interests; impose威 on the enemy and cities can be taken and states overthrown. Administer rewards without fixed law and hang decrees without governance. Make the multitudes act as one person. Strike them into action by deeds, not by words; strike them with gain and do not announce the harm. Cast them into a lost ground and then they will live; plunge them into death ground and then they will die. Only when a host is driven into danger can victory and defeat be decided. Thus the affairs of war lie in feigning compliance with the enemy’s intent, compressing the enemy’s direction into one, slaying commanders a thousand miles away—this is the cunning that achieves results.

Therefore on the day one mobilizes, level the passes and break the tally-chits so their envoys cannot get through; be severe on the altars and in halls to punish deeds. When the enemy opens and closes, rush in quickly; first seize what he loves; give him little time; press close on his heels to decide the engagement. Therefore at first be like a maiden when the enemy opens his door; later be like a rabbit from which there is no escape and the enemy cannot resist.

points.title: Different natures of the Nine Grounds
points.body: The nine grounds are not merely terrain types; they are defined by distance from home, lines of communication, mutual interests, and the relationship between enemy and friendly forces.

points.title: Speed is decisive
points.body: Speed is used to exploit the enemy’s unpreparedness and attack where he is unguarded, not as reckless movement divorced from supply and order.

points.title: Deep penetration concentrates forces
points.body: Retreat routes, distance and resources change soldiers’ psychology; leaders must understand how the situation affects unit cohesion.

points.title: The serpent analogy
points.body: Mutual support between front and rear does not occur spontaneously; it is produced by command, terrain, and shared stakes that make the group respond as a whole.

points.title: Act on openings
points.body: Rules give orientation, but action must follow the enemy’s openings and battlefield movement rather than a fixed form.

en.summary: On the surface this chapter treats conditions for using fire, but its real emphasis is that tools, timing and responses must align. Fire attacks have different targets and require supplies and suitable weather; after ignition commanders must watch the enemy’s reaction to decide whether to follow up. Even a successful assault is wasted if its gains are not secured. The chapter closes by raising caution in warfare to a political ethic: ruler and general must not wage war in sudden anger, because emotions recover but lost states and lives do not.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — Fire Attack: Timing, Tools, and Restraint
en.seoDescription: Five kinds of fire attack, required conditions and timing, how to respond, and why leaders must avoid anger and consolidate victory.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In all there are five kinds of fire attack: first, fire against the people; second, fire on stores; third, fire on wagons; fourth, fire on magazines; fifth, fire on the troops. To employ fire one must have a cause; smoke and flames must be properly prepared. There is a season to set fire, and there are days on which to kindle it. 'Season' means dry weather. 'Day' means when the moon is in the constellations Ji, Bi, Yi, or Zhen. On the days of these four lunar mansions, winds arise.

In any fire attack, one must respond according to the five variations of fire: if fire breaks out inside, then respond early from without; if fire breaks out and the enemy troops remain calm, wait and do not attack; when the fire reaches its peak, one may follow and exploit it; if one cannot follow, then stop. Fire can be started from outside without waiting for an internal blaze—start it at the proper time. If the fire is upwind, do not attack downwind. A long daytime wind will often cease at night. Every army must know the five changes of fire and guard against them accordingly. Thus to use fire in support of an attack is a clear tactic; to use water in support is a strong measure. Water can cut off, but it cannot seize.

When one wins in battle and seizes the prize but does not consolidate the achievement, the result is harmful; this is called 'wasteful lingering.' Therefore an enlightened ruler considers it carefully, and a good general finishes the work. Do not move without advantage, do not employ forces without gain, do not engage unless there is peril. A ruler must not raise troops in anger; a commander must not bring on battle out of resentment. Act when it is advantageous; desist when it is not. Anger can return to joy, resentment can return to pleasure, but a fallen state cannot be restored and the dead cannot be brought back to life. Therefore the wise ruler is cautious and the good general is vigilant—this is the way to secure the state and preserve the army.

points.title: Fire requires cause and readiness
points.body: Any tool demands the right conditions, supplies and timing; a method without supporting elements cannot produce effective action.

points.title: Respond to changing conditions
points.body: After fire starts, do not attack mechanically; observe whether the enemy is disordered and whether the fire’s force can be exploited, then decide whether to press on or to stop.

points.title: Water can cut off but cannot seize
points.body: Different means have different operational limits. Being able to interrupt is not the same as being able to capture; do not confuse functions.

points.title: Victory without consolidation is loss
points.body: If you win but do not organize and secure the gains, prior costs may become wasted expenditure.

points.title: Do not wage war in anger
points.body: Major, irreversible decisions must not be driven by transient emotions; caution in warfare is a safeguard for lives and the state.

en.fullTitle: On the Use of Spies — Chapter Thirteen
en.summary: The final chapter argues from the high cost of war to demonstrate the value of intelligence: if one begrudges titles and rewards and therefore fails to invest in spies, leaving soldiers and civilians to endure prolonged expense, that is both cruel and foolish. Foreknowledge cannot be obtained from gods, analogy, or conjecture; it must come from people who know the enemy's situation. There are five kinds of spies—local, inside, turned, expendable, and returning—each with a distinct function; among them, the turned spy is the pivot for identifying and using the enemy's intelligence network. Intelligence work requires wisdom, benevolence, subtlety, and strict secrecy.
en.seoTitle: Sun Tzu — The Use of Spies: Intelligence and Counterintelligence
en.seoDescription: Chapter on intelligence: five types of spies, the central role of turned agents, and the necessity of human sources, secrecy and wise handling.

segments.text: Sun Tzu said: In general, when mobilizing an army of a hundred thousand and campaigning a thousand li, the people's expenses and the state's provisions amount to a thousand pieces of gold a day; internal and external unrest follow, the people are exhausted along the roads, and seven hundred thousand households are unable to attend to their affairs. To wage war for years in pursuit of a single day's victory, yet begrudge a hundred pieces of gold in titles and rewards and so remain ignorant of the enemy's condition, is the height of inhumanity; such a person is not a commander of men, not a helper to his sovereign, and not a master of victory. Therefore an enlightened ruler and a worthy general who can move and defeat others, with success arising from foreknowledge, are those who act on prior knowledge. Foreknowledge cannot be obtained from ghosts or spirits, inferred from analogy, or verified by calculation; it must be obtained from people who know the enemy's situation.

Hence there are five kinds of spies: local spies, inside spies, turned spies, expendable (dead) spies, and returning (living) spies. When all five kinds of spies are active and no one knows their methods, this is called 'divine order' and is the sovereign's treasure. Local spies are used because they are countrymen; inside spies are used because they are officials; turned spies are used because they are enemy agents; expendable spies are used to spread false stories outside so that our spies learn them and then pass them to the enemy; returning spies are those who come back with reports.

Therefore, of the affairs of the three armies nothing is more intimate than spies, nothing is awarded more richly than spies, and nothing must be kept more secret than spies. Without sage wisdom one cannot employ spies; without benevolence and righteousness one cannot make use of spies; without subtlety one cannot obtain true reports from spies. How subtle! How subtle! There is nothing in which spies are not employed. If an espionage matter has not yet begun but is heard of in advance, both the spy and those to whom he reported will die.

Whenever the army intends to strike, a city to be taken, or men to be killed, one must first learn the names of the defending general, his attendants, ushers, gatekeepers, and household servants; our spies must be ordered to obtain these names. One must also seek out enemy agents who come to spy on us, reward them, guide them, and then release them; thus a turned spy can be obtained and put to use. Through this, local and inside spies can be identified and employed; through this, expendable spies can be made to convey falsehoods to the enemy; through this, returning spies can be made to report on schedule. The ruler must know the affairs of all five kinds of spies; such knowledge depends on turned spies, and therefore turned spies must be rewarded generously.

In former times, when the Shang arose, Yi Zhi served in Xia; when the Zhou rose, Lü Ya served in Shang. Therefore an enlightened ruler and a worthy general who can employ the wisest as spies will surely accomplish great deeds. This is the essence of warfare, the reliance of the three armies when they move.

points.title: Foreknowledge Must Come from People
points.body: Reliable intelligence must have human, traceable sources and direct contacts; it cannot be replaced by superstition, imagination, or unverified analogies.

points.title: All Five Spies Working Together
points.body: Different classes of agents must operate together to form a network that verifies information, influences the enemy, feeds deception, and returns reports.

points.title: Nothing Closer Than Spies
points.body: Intelligence sits closest to command and therefore requires corresponding trust, resources, secrecy, and ethical handling.

points.title: Turned Spies Are the Pivot
points.body: Identifying and using enemy agents who can be turned reduces infiltration risk and enables understanding and exploitation of the opponent's system.

points.title: Employ the Wisest as Spies
points.body: A ruler and general who employ the wisest as spies can achieve great deeds; intelligence is the essential basis on which the whole army acts.

ja.group: 廟算（国家レベルの算策）
ja.summary: 本篇は戦争を国家の存亡と国民の生死に関わる重大事と定義し、意思決定の前に「道・天・地・将・法」の五事で共通の尺度を定め、七計で敵我を比較することを説く。比較は単なる静的評価ではなく、利用可能な利を見極め勢に応じて機を制する方策を組み立てるためのものだ。詭道に関する諸法は情報と認知の操作に属し、最終的には未戦の段階での綿密な算段に帰着する。条件・準備・判断が充実していれば、勝敗はより予見しやすくなる。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子・始計：戦前に勝敗を決める五事と七計
ja.seoDescription: 戦争を国家の重大事と定義し、五事と七計で敵我を比較。詭道を含む情報操作と未戦の算段が勝敗を左右する。

segments.text: 孫子は言う。兵は国家の重大事であり、生死がかかる場であり、存亡に関わる道であって、これを軽んじてはならない。ゆえに五事をもってこれを論じ、七計をもってこれを比較し、その実情を探るのである。すなわち第一は道、第二は天、第三は地、第四は将、第五は法である。

道とは、国民が君と意を同じくし、ともに死に、ともに生き、危険を恐れない状態をいう。天とは陰陽や寒暑、季節や時節のことをいう。地とは地形の高低・遠近・険易・広狭および生死にかかわる点をいう。将とは智・信・仁・勇・厳の資質をいう。法とは法制、官道、主用──つまり規律・補給路・制度や運用のことである。これら五つは将ならずとも皆知るところである。これを知る者は勝ち、知らぬ者は勝てない。ゆえに七計によってこれらを比較して実情を問う。すなわち、主はどちらが道に適っているか、将はどちらが有能か、天地はどちらが有利か、法令はどちらが行われているか、兵力はどちらが強いか、兵卒はどちらが鍛錬されているか、賞罰はどちらが明確か。私はこれによって勝敗を見定める。

もし将が私の計を聞き、それを用いれば必ず勝つ。そういう将は留めよ。将が私の計を聞かず、それを用いれば必ず敗れる。そういう将は去らせよ。計を利によって聞かせ、かくして勢を為してその外を補助する。勢とは利に因って機を制することである。兵とは詭道である。ゆえに、能力があるように見せて無能に見せかけ、用いるように見せて用いないように見せ、近いものを遠く見せ、遠いものを近く見せる。利で誘い、混乱させて奪い、充実しているときには備えさせ、強いときは避け、怒らせてこれを挫き、卑しい者をして驕らせ、安逸にある者を労させ、親しい者を離反させる。備えなき所を攻め、意表を突く。これが兵家の勝ち方であり、前もって広めてはならない。
戦う前に宮中で算した段階で勝てる者は、算が多い者である。戦う前に宮中で算して勝てない者は、算が少ない者である。算の多い者が勝ち、算の少ない者は勝てない。ましてや算のない者はなおさらである。私はこれによって勝敗を見通す。

points.title: 兵は国家の重大事
points.body: 戦争は将個人の冒険に留まらない。公共資源や生死、政権の存亡に関わるため、まず慎重な検討が求められる。

points.title: 五事と七計
points.body: 五事は観察の視点を示し、七計は敵我を項目ごとに比較する。両者を併用することで戦前の判断枠組みが構成される。

points.title: 利に因りて機を制す
points.body: 計画は現実の利害や条件に応じて調整されるべきだ。権の行使は恣意ではなく、具体的情勢に基づく衡量によって行われる。

points.title: 詭道と示し方
points.body: 能と不能、用と不用、近と遠を逆に示すことは相手の判断を揺さぶり、隙を露出させるための情報・認知操作である。

points.title: 廟算で先に勝つ
points.body: 真の勝勢は行動以前に形成される。算（綿密な検討）が多いほど条件を洗い出し比較でき、勝敗はより予見しやすくなる。

ja.summary: 本篇は戦争の時間的・経済的コストを論じる。一旦大軍を動かせば輸送・装備・徴発・物価上昇が国家力を継続的に消耗する。戦術が巧妙でも長期化すれば勝利の価値は薄れる。ゆえに用兵は迅速に目的を達し、補給線を可能な限り短縮することが重要である。敵の物資や人員の接収は単なる略奪ではなく、報奨・整編・転用を含めて行い、敵を倒して自国を弱めないことを目指す。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子・作戦：戦争のコストと速戦の要諦
ja.seoDescription: 戦争が国家にもたらす時間的・経済的負担と、速やかな勝利と敵資源の活用による補給節約の重要性を説く章。

segments.text: 孫子は言う。凡そ用兵の法は、車を馳せ千駟、革車千乗、甲を帯び十万、千里にわたって糧を供給するならば、すなわち内外の費用、賓客の接遇、膠漆の用材、車甲の保存などに日に千金を費やして、ようやく十万の師を挙げることができる。戦に臨むにあたっては勝つことを尊ぶ。長引けば兵は鈍り鋭気は挫け、城を攻めれば力は尽き、師を長く晒せば国家の費用は不足する。兵を鈍らせ鋭気を挫き、力を屈し財を尽くせば、諸侯はその弊に乗じて起こる。たとえ智ある者あれど、後を善くすることはできない。故に兵は拙速を聞くことあれど、巧みにして久しきを見ない。兵久しくして国に利ある者は未だかつていない。故に用兵の害を尽くして知らぬ者は、則ち用兵の利を尽くして知ること能わず。
善く兵を用いる者は、徭役を再び課さず、糧を三年にわたって取り立てさせない。国から無理に取り立てるのではなく、敵から糧を得て用いるので、ゆえに軍の食糧は足りうる。
国が軍に貧するのは、遠くから輸送するからである。遠距離輸送すれば百姓は貧しくなる。軍が近くにいると物売りは値を高め、値高により百姓の財は尽き、財が尽きれば徭役に追われる。力が屈し財が尽きれば、中央の地は内的に家々が虚しくなる。百姓の負担は十のうち七を失い、公の費用は壊れた車や休める馬、甲冑や弩矢、戟や盾、櫓、牛や大車などに費やされ、十のうち六を失う。
ゆえに智将は敵の糧を得ることに努める。敵の食糧一鐘は我が二十鐘に当たり、敵の萁稈一石は我が二十石に当たる。
ゆえに敵を殺すのは怒によるものであり、敵の利を取るのは財である。車戦において車を十乗以上得たら、先に取った者に賞を与え、その旌旗を取り替える。捕えた車を混ぜて乗せ、兵をよく養えば、これをもって敵に勝ちながら益々強くするという。
ゆえに兵は勝つことを尊び、長引くことを尊ばない。ゆえに兵を知る将は民の生死を司り、国家の安危を左右する主である。

points.title: 兵は勝ちを重んじ、久戦を重んじない
points.body: 本章は軽率を勧めるものではない。むしろ長期化による消耗が兵を鈍らせ、鋭気を挫き、力を疲弊させ、財を尽きさせ、その隙に第三勢力が付け入ることを指摘している。

points.title: 用兵の害を十分に知る
points.body: 可能な利益のみを見て直接費用・間接費用を無視すれば、用兵の是非は判断できない。リスクの認識が利益判断の前提となる。

points.title: 敵の糧に依る
points.body: 遠距離補給は負担を国内の民衆に転嫁する。補給線を短縮し、既存の資源や敵資源を利用することが戦争の総コストを下げる手段である。

points.title: 敵を勝ち取り自らを強くする
points.body: 敵の車や戦力を獲得したら旗を付け替え混成して用い、俘虜や離反兵を手厚く扱って養成する。これは資源の転用と組織的吸収の考え方を示す。

ja.summary: 本章は「全勝」の観点を示す。最高の勝利とは正面衝突の多勝ではなく、相手の計略や同盟を崩し、抵抗力を奪うことである。攻城は費用と損耗が大きく、最終手段に限られる。篇は兵力配分や君主と将軍の関係、勝利を見極める条件を扱い、政治的指導は軍事の専門に越権介入してはならず、将は敵我や兵力、時機、組織の意志を理解しなければならないと説く。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子『謀攻』第三章の現代日本語訳と要点
ja.seoDescription: 孫子『謀攻』第三章を現代日本語で訳出。戦わずして勝つ全勝観や伐謀・伐交の序列、君主と将の関係を解説します。

segments.text: 孫子は言う。凡そ兵を用いる法は、国を全うすることを上となし、国を破ることはその次である。軍を全うすることを上となし、軍を破ることはその次である。旅を全うすることを上となし、旅を破ることはその次である。卒（兵）を全うすることを上となし、卒を破ることはその次である。伍を全うすることを上となし、伍を破ることはその次である。ゆえに百戦百勝することは最上の善ではない。戦わずして人の兵を屈することが、最上の善である。
ゆえに上の兵は謀を伐つこと、その次は交を伐つこと、その次は兵を伐つこと、もっとも劣るのは城を攻めることである。攻城の法はやむを得ない場合のためである。櫓や攻具を修め、器械を整えるには三月を要し、さらに城壁に迫るにはさらに三月を要する。将が怒りに勝てず無理を強いて兵をかき付け、兵の三分の一を失っても城を落とせないことがある。これが攻城の災いである。
ゆえに兵を善く用いる者は、人の兵を屈するが戦わず、人の城を取るが攻めず、人の国を滅ぼすが長期にわたらない。必ず「全」をもって天下で争う。それゆえ兵を疲弊させずに利を全うできる。これが謀攻の法である。
ゆえに兵を用いる法は、相手が十ならこれを囲み、五ならこれを攻め、倍（こちらが倍の兵力）なら分割し、互角なら戦い、少なければ守り、及ばなければ避ける。小さな敵が堅固であるのは、大きな敵によって捕らえられるためである。
将とは国の輔（補佐）である。補佐が周到であれば国は必ず強く、補佐に隙があれば国は必ず弱くなる。
ゆえに君が軍を憂う理由は三つある。軍が進むべきでないのに進めと言い、軍が退くべきでないのに退けと言う――これを縻（縛）すという。三軍の事を知らずして三軍の政を同じくするなら、軍士は惑う。三軍の権（機微）を知らずして三軍の任を同じくするなら、軍士は疑う。三軍が既に惑い且つ疑えば、諸侯の難事が到来する。これを乱軍引勝という。
ゆえに勝利を知ることは五つある。戦うべきか否かを知る者は勝ち、衆寡（兵力の多寡）の用い方を識る者は勝ち、上下が同じ欲（志）を持つ者は勝ち、虞（準備）をもって不意を待つ者は勝ち、将が能くして君がこれを抑えない者は勝つ。これら五つが勝利を知る道である。
ゆえに曰く、彼を知り己を知れば、百戦して危うからず。彼を知らずして己を知れば、一勝一負。彼も己も知らなければ、戦うたびに必ず危うい。

points.title: 不戦而屈人之兵（戦わずして人の兵を屈する）
points.body: 最上の善とは勝利の回数で測るのではなく、最小の破壊で目的を達することを基準とする。

points.title: 上兵伐謀（上位の手段は謀を破る）
points.body: 手段には明確な序列がある：まず計略を破り、次に外交（同盟）を断ち、さらに野戦、攻城は最後の手段である。

points.title: 必以全爭於天下（全を以て競う）
points.body: 『全』とは単なる不戦ではなく、国・軍・利益の可用性を保ち、成功が自軍の消耗によらないことを意味する。

points.title: 君之所以患於軍者三（君主が軍を憂う三つの理由）
points.body: 進退の条件、組織運営、指揮権の機微を理解せず越権介入すると、軍は惑い疑い、秩序を失う。

points.title: 知彼知己（彼を知り己を知る）
points.body: 勝利の理解はスローガンではなく、可戦性の識別、兵力運用、上下の一致、準備と奇襲への対応、指揮の自主性の総合的判断である。

ja.summary: 本章は、コントロールできる事柄とそうでない事柄の境界を論じる。まず自らを不敗にする条件を整えることは己の責任であり、敵が勝ち得る状況を露呈するかどうかは敵に委ねられる。善い戦い手は名声や大きな博奕を追わず、条件が整った安全な戦局を選択する。度・量・数・称・勝の順序は、地理・資源・兵力・比較評価を積み重ねて勝敗を導く手順を示す。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子 軍形（第四）—不敗を築き勝機を待つ
ja.seoDescription: 自軍をまず不敗にし、敵の露呈する勝機を待つ。勝利は地形・資源・数・比較の段階的計算から生まれると説く章。

segments.text: 孫子は言う：古の善く戦う者は、まず自らを敗れ得ない状態に整え、敵の勝ち得る時を待った。敗れ得ないことは己にあり、勝ち得ることは敵にある。したがって善く戦う者は、不敗を為すことはできても、敵を必ず勝ち得る者に変えることはできない。ゆえに言う：勝ちうることは知り得ても、それを作り出すことはできない。
敗れ得ないものは守りにあり、勝ち得るものは攻めにある。守れば不足し、攻めれば余る。守りに巧みな者は九地の下に隠れ、攻めに巧みな者は九天の上に動く。ゆえに自らを保ちつつ完全な勝利を得ることができる。
人々が知るような勝ち方を見るだけでは、本当に巧みな者とは言えない。戦って勝ち、天下が『善い』と言うのも、本当に巧みな者のやり方ではない。だから秋のわずかな毛を挙げて多力とはせず、日月を見ることを明眼とはせず、雷霆を聞くことを鋭い耳とはしない。

古にいう『善く戦う者』とは、勝ちやすき所に勝つ者である。ゆえに善戦者の勝には智の名も勇の功もない。したがってその戦いの勝ちは誤りがない。誤りがないとは、彼らの置くところは必ず勝ち、すでに敗れている者に対して勝つということである。ゆえに善く戦う者は、敗れない地位に立ち、敵の敗れを見逃さない。だから勝つ兵は先に勝ちを得てから戦いを求め、敗れる兵は先に戦ってから勝ちを求める。兵を善く用いる者は道を修め法を守るので、勝敗を左右することができる。
兵法には一に度、二に量、三に数、四に称、五に勝がある。地は度を生み、度は量を生み、量は数を生み、数は称を生み、称は勝を生む。したがって勝つ軍は、まるで鎰で銖を量るかのごとく（大きな単位で小さなものを扱うがごとく）振る舞い、敗れる軍は銖で鎰を量るがごとし。勝者の戦いは、堆積した水を千仞の渓に決して放つがごとき形である。

points.title: まず不敗を築く
points.body: まず自分の防護、制度、準備を整え、外部の機会を待つ。これはリスク管理が利益追求に先行することを意味する。

points.title: 不敗は己に、勝機は敵にある
points.body: 失敗を避けることは比較的自分でコントロールできる。一方で相手を打ち破るかどうかは、相手が条件を露呈するかどうかに依存する。

points.title: 勝ちやすい地点を選ぶ
points.body: 巧者の真価は、劣勢な状況で名を求めることではなく、既に勝勢が整っている戦いを選択する点にある。

points.title: 勝つ軍は先に勝ちを確保する
points.body: 行動は既に優勢が形成されてからの最後の表現であり、行動そのもので優勢が生まれると賭けるものではない。

points.title: 度・量・数・称が勝利を生む
points.body: 地形の尺度から資源の容量、兵力の数、比較評価へと段階的に積み上げる計算が最終的に勝敗を決する。

ja.summary: 本篇は組織と指揮を通じて「勢」の形成を論じる。大勢を治めることは少数を治めることと同じであり、その鍵は編制と合図にある。戦いの変化は多様だが、基本要素は正と奇の反復的な組合せにある。勢は抽象的な気勢ではなく、位置・速度・リズム・条件を組み合わせて解き放たれる力である。優れた指導者は個々の勇気を求めるだけでなく、平凡な者でも適切な位置に置けば全体として効果を発揮するよう環境を設計する。
ja.seoDescription: 編制・形・奇正・虚実を通じて「勢」を作り出す方法を解説。リズムと配置で普通の兵でも全体効果を発揮させる指導の要点。

segments.text: 孫子は言う。多くの兵を治めることは少数を治めることと同じであり、そのためのものが分数（編成）である。多くの者を闘わせることは少数を闘わせることと同じであり、それが形と名（形名）である。三軍の兵をして、敵を必ず受けさせて敗れさせないものは奇と正である。兵を加えるありさまは、丸石で卵を投げるようなもの、すなわち虚と実である。

凡て戦う者は、正で相対し、奇で勝つ。したがって奇を出すことに巧みな者は、天地のごとく尽きず、江海の水のごとく枯れない。終わればまた始まるのは日月のごとく、死して復生するのは四時のごとし。音は五を越えず、五音の変化は聞き尽くせない。色は五を越えず、五色の変化は見尽くせない。味は五を越えず、五味の変化は味わい尽くせない。戦の勢も奇と正を越えず、奇正の変化は尽きることがない。奇と正は互いに生じ合い、循環に終わりはない。誰がこれを尽くすことができようか。
激しい水流の速さが石を流すようにするのが勢であり、猛禽の鋭い速さが物を打ち砕くのが節である。ゆえに戦に巧みな者は、その勢を険しくし、その節を短くする。勢は張り詰めた弩（わな）のようであり、節は発射の機構の瞬間のようである。
紛々と入り乱れているようでも、闘いは乱れてはならない。渾々として形が混然としているようでも、形は円満であって敗れてはならない。乱れは治（整えられた編成）から生じ、臆病は勇から生じ、弱さは強さから生じる。治と乱は数（配分・編制）に関することであり、勇と怯は勢に関することであり、強と弱は形に関することである。
ゆえに敵を巧みに動かす者は、形を示せば敵は必ずそれに従い、与えれば敵は必ずそれを取りに来る。利益をもって動かし、兵をもってそれを待つのである。
ゆえに戦いに巧みな者は、勢に求め、人の責を問いはしない。だからこそ人を選び勢を任せられるのだ。勢に任せるとは、人を戦わせるに際して木や石を転がすようなものである。木や石の性質は、安ければ静まり、危うければ動き、角ばっていれば止まり、円ければ行く。ゆえに戦いの巧者の勢は、千仞の山で円石を転がすがごときものなのである。

points.title: 編成と形名
points.body: 大きな組織が指揮可能かどうかは、階層的な編成、責任単位、統一された合図システムによって決まる。

points.title: 正で合わせ、奇で勝つ
points.body: 正と奇は互いに転化する配置であり、ある手段を永久に奇策と決めつけるものではない。

points.title: 勢は険しく、節は短く
points.body: 力は短く効果的な解放点に集中すべきであり、張った弩を放つように。リズムを引き延ばすと本来の優位は散逸する。

points.title: 形を作り、利で誘う
points.body: 目に見える形勢と利益の誘因によって相手の反応を誘導し、用意した兵力でその行動を受け止める。

points.title: 勢に求め、人を責めず
points.body: 指導者の責任は人を選び勢を任せ、条件を配置することであり、システムの失敗を個人にすべて帰することではない。

ja.summary: 本章の核心は主導権を握り、敵を自らが仕組んだ流れに沿わせることである。利害の操作、速度、陽動と隠蔽を用いて敵の注意を分散させ、我が方は決定点に兵力を集中させる。兵形の究極は無形にあり、敵にどこへ資源を割くべきか判断させないことが最良である。末節は水の喩えを用いる：水は高きを避け低きを往き、兵は実を避け虚を撃つ。方法は固定すべきでなく、敵と環境に応じて常に変化させねばならない。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子『虚実』第六章：無形で敵を制する戦術
ja.seoDescription: 先手を取り敵を誘導し虚を突いて一点に集中する。無形の兵法で敵の備えを分散させ勝機を掴む方法を説く章。

segments.text: 孫子は言う。戦場に先んじて陣取り敵を待つ者はゆとりがあり、後から戦地に到って戦いに駆けつける者は疲弊する。ゆえに、よく戦う者は他を赴かせて自ら赴かれない。
敵を自ら来させることができるのは利益を与えるからであり、敵を来させないのは害を与えるからである。ゆえに敵のゆとりを疲れさせ、満腹の者を飢えさせ、安んじている者を動かす。敵の行かぬ所から出て、敵の意の及ばぬ所へ向かうのだ。
千里を行っても疲れないのは人のいない地を行くからである。攻めて必ず奪うのは敵の守らぬ所を攻めるからであり、守って必ず堅固なのは敵が攻めぬ所を守るからである。ゆえに善く攻むる者は敵に何処を守るか知られず、善く守る者は敵に何処を攻めるか知られない。きわめて微細であって形は無形に至り、まことに神妙であって声は無きがごとし。それゆえ敵の生死を司ることができるのだ。
前へ出て阻止できないのはその虚を衝くからであり、退いて追えないのは速さが及ばないからである。したがって我が戦いたければ、敵がいかに高塁深溝を築いていようとも彼らが必ず救援する所を攻めれば戦わざるを得なくなる。逆に我が戦いたくなければ、たとえ地に線を画して守っていても、敵は行くところを外されて戦えなくなる。

ゆえに人に形を見せ我は無形ならば、我は集中し敵は分散する。我は一に専念し、敵は十に分かれる。十が一を攻めれば我は多数で敵は少数である。多数を以て少数を撃つことができれば、我が対する相手は限定される。われが戦う地点が知られなければ敵の備えは多くなり、その結果われが実際に相対する敵は少なくなる。前を備えれば後が手薄になり、後を備えれば前が手薄になり、左を備えれば右が手薄になり、右を備えれば左が手薄になる。すべてを備えればすべてが手薄となる。『手薄な者』は備えられる者を指し、『多数』は人を我に備えさせる者を指す。
ゆえに戦う地点を知り戦う日を知らば千里を隔てて会戦に臨める。戦う地点も日も知らなければ左は右を救えず右は左を救えず前は後を救えず後は前を救えない。まして遠方は数十里、近方は数里であればなおさらである。わが見立てでは、越人の兵がいかに多くとも勝敗に何の助けとなろうか。ゆえに言う、勝利は我がものにしうる。敵がいかに衆であっても争わせないことができる。
ゆえに策をめぐらして損得の計を知り、行動して動静の理を悟り、形を整えて死生の地を見定め、角によって有余不足の処を知る。よって兵の形の究極は無形に至る。無形であれば深い間者も窺えず、智者も謀れない。形に拠って衆に勝利を置けば衆はそれを知り得ない。人は皆我が勝つ形を知っても、我が勝利を制する形を知らない。ゆえに戦に勝てばそれは再現されず、形は無窮に応じて変化する。
兵の形は水に象えられる。水の流れは高きを避けて低きに向かう。兵の勝ちは実を避けて虚を撃つ。水は地に因って行を制し、兵は敵に因って勝を制す。ゆえに兵に恒常の勢も恒常の形もなく、敵に応じて変化して勝つ者を『神』と称する。五行に常勝なし、四時に常位なし。日には長短があり、月には死生がある。

points.title: 致人而不致於人
points.body: 主導権を取るとは単に先に動くことだけでなく、時間・位置・資源の配分において敵に対応させることを意味する。

points.title: 攻其所必救
points.body: 敵の強点を正面突破する必要はない。敵がどうしても救援する地点を突くことで戦いを強いる。

points.title: 我專而敵分
points.body: 主攻を隠して敵を多方面に備えさせ、特定の一点に兵力を集中して多数で少数を撃つ。

points.title: 形兵之極，至於無形
points.body: 配置や動きに読めるパターンを与えず、情報優位が敵に逆用されるのを防ぐことが重要である。

points.title: 兵形象水
points.body: 勝ち方は地形と敵に応じて変えるべきであり、過去の成功形を固定的に繰り返すと効力を失う。

ja.summary: 本篇は軍隊が集結して有利な位置を争う際の難題を扱う。迂回を直進に転じ、災いを利として利用する計を説き、誘因・路線・速度・後勤を結び付けて先着を図ることを強調する。単に速さを追うと輜重を失い部隊が分裂する危険がある。『風』『林』『火』『山』の節奏、金鼓と旌旗による一体的指揮、士気と体力の管理、佯敗や餌兵、帰師や窮寇への克制などが述べられる。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子・軍爭（第七章）— 迂直と行軍の節奏
ja.seoDescription: 軍の集結から有利地点の争奪まで。迂回を利に変える策、速度と補給、士気管理や風林火山の行動原則を説く章。

segments.text: 孫子は言う。兵を用いる法では、将は君の命を受け、軍を合わせ衆を聚め、交わり和して宿営することが基本であるが、なかでも軍争ほど難しいことはない。軍争の難しさは、迂遠を直進に変え、災いを利益に転じる点にある。したがって道を迂らせて利で誘い、後発の者を動かさせ、先んじて到る――これを以て迂直の計を知る者である。

ゆえに軍争は利益をもたらす一方で危険も伴う。全軍を挙げて利を争えば間に合わず、軍を分けて利を争えば輜重を失う。したがって鎧をまとめ、昼夜休まず、倍の速さで強行軍する。百里先の利を争えば、三軍の将が捕らえられるおそれがある。強健な者は先に進み、疲れた者は後に続くため、到着できるのは十人に一人である。五十里先の利を争えば先鋒の将を失い、到着できるのは半数である。三十里先の利を争えば三分の二が到着する。ゆえに軍は輜重がなければ滅び、食糧がなければ滅び、備蓄がなければ滅ぶ。諸侯の謀略を知らなければ前もって同盟を結べず、山林・険阻・沼沢の地形を知らなければ行軍できず、土地に詳しい案内人を用いなければ地の利を得られない。
兵は詐を以て立ち、利を以て動き、分合を以て変ずる。ゆえにその疾きは風のごとく、その徐なるは林のごとく、侵掠するは火のごとく、動かざるは山のごとく、察しがたきは陰のごとく、動くは雷震のごとし。郷を掠し衆を分かち、地を広げて利を分ち、権を懸して動く。迂直の計を先に知る者が勝つ、これが軍争の法である。
『軍政』に曰く「言葉が互いに聞こえぬゆえに金鼓を置き、視線が互いに見えぬゆえに旌旗を立てる」と。金鼓や旌旗は、民衆の耳目を一つにするためのものである。民が一つに専念すれば、勇者は単独で進めず、怯む者は単独で退けない。これが衆を用いる法である。ゆえに夜戦では金鼓を多くし、昼戦では旌旗を多く用いて、人々の耳目を変えるのである。

三軍の気勢は奪うことができ、将軍の心も奪える。ゆえに朝は気が鋭く、昼は気が惰り、夕は帰還の気になる。よって巧みに兵を用いる者は、その鋭きを避け、その惰れて帰る時を撃つ――これが気を操る者である。秩序ある態勢をもって乱れを待ち、静けさをもって喧騒を待つ――これが心を操る者である。近きものをもって遠きを待ち、安らかな者をもって労する者を待ち、満ちた者をもって飢えた者を待つ――これが力を操る者である。正々堂々たる旗を求めず、堂々たる陣を撃たない――これが変化を治める者である。
ゆえに用兵の原則は次のとおりである。高地を占める敵に向かって進むな。丘を背にする敵を迎え撃つな。偽りの退却を追うな。鋭気盛んな部隊を攻撃するな。囮として差し出された部隊に食いつくな。帰還する軍の道を塞ぐな。軍を包囲するときは必ず逃げ道を残せ。窮地に陥った敵を追いつめるな。これが用兵の原則である。

points.title: 以迂為直，以患為利
points.body: 間接的な進路が相手の判断を変え時間を稼げるなら、結果的に先着するための直接的な手段になり得る。

points.title: 軍爭為利，軍爭為危
points.body: 機会を追う行動は速度を生むが隊列の延長や補給喪失を招く――利益と危険は常に表裏一体である。

points.title: 風林火山
points.body: 迅速、徐行、侵掠、不動という節奏を目的に応じて切り替えることが重要で、一律の急速さを追うべきではない。

points.title: 一民之耳目
points.body: 金鼓や旌旗という共通の合図は、個々の勇気や怯懦を組織行動へと変換し、部隊の一体性を保つ手段である。

points.title: 治氣、治心、治力、治變
points.body: 敵の気力・心情・体力・陣形の変化を見極め、それぞれに応じて待つ・避く・攻めるを使い分けることが勝利を左右する。

ja.summary: 本篇は原則を情勢から切り離してはならないことを強調する。ある道を通らない、ある軍を撃たない、ある城地を争わない、さらには君の命に従わないことさえ、一般的な規則を機械的に適用することを避けるためである。成熟した判断は利益の中に潜む危険を見出し、害の中に解決策を探す。最後に将の五つの危険を列挙し、勇気や生への執着、短気、清廉、民への愛情が節度を失うと敵に利用されることを示す。
ja.seoTitle: 孫子・九変（第八）— 臨機応変の兵法と将の五つの危険
ja.seoDescription: 第八篇「九変」は、原則を情勢に合わせる重要性を説き、行動しない選択や利害併考の必要性を示す。戦略判断で利と害を同時に考え、敵に付け入られない備えを強調する。
